title: What is the R&D payroll tax offset for startups?
description: A qualified small business startup can elect to apply up to $500,000 a year of its research credit against employer Social Security and Medicare taxes.
summary: The R&D payroll tax offset lets a U.S. startup that is a qualified small business, with under $5 million in current-year gross receipts and no gross receipts before its five-year window, elect on Form 6765 to apply up to $500,000 per year of its federal research credit against employer Social Security and Medicare taxes, claimed quarterly on Form 8974.

body.text: The R&D payroll tax offset lets a U.S. startup that is a qualified small business, with under $5 million in current-year gross receipts and no gross receipts before its five-year window, elect on Form 6765 to apply up to $500,000 per year of its federal research credit against employer Social Security and Medicare taxes, claimed quarterly on Form 8974.
Summary

The R&D payroll tax offset lets a young, small business use part of its federal research credit against the employer's share of payroll taxes instead of waiting for income tax liability. Under IRC §41(h) and §3111(f), a qualified small business (defined as an eligible entity with gross receipts under $5 million for the current tax year, and no gross receipts for any tax year before the five-tax-year period ending with that tax year) may elect to apply up to $500,000 of its research credit per year for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 ($250,000 per year for tax years beginning after December 31, 2015, and before January 1, 2023). The election is made on Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, attached to a timely filed original income tax return (including extensions), and the credit is claimed on Form 8974, Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities, filed with the quarterly payroll tax return (such as Form 941) starting with the first calendar quarter that begins after the income tax return making the election is filed.

items: The worked example's assertion of a $100,000 regular research credit on $500,000 of qualified research expenses (QREs) is mathematically impossible under the statutory minimum base amount rule of IRC §41(c)(2) (under which the maximum regular credit is capped at 10% of current-year QREs, or $50,000);

The reference to a "$250,000 quarterly" maximum cash benefit conflates the annual statutory election limit ($500,000) with the per-quarter Social Security tax offset cap on Form 8974 ($250,000 per quarter against the 6.2% OASDI tax before excess credit flows against the 1.45% Medicare tax);
The IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) "Tier 1" compliance issue designation was formally discontinued in August 2012;
The United Kingdom HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) audit disallowance statistics quoted do not match HMRC's published Mandatory Random Enquiry Programme (MREP) figures; and

The IRC §280C(c) reduced credit election analysis requires updating to reflect the enactment of Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025), which restored domestic research expensing under IRC §174A and amended §280C(c) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.

body.text: Why the payroll offset exists

The federal research credit under IRC §41 is a component of the general business credit under IRC §38, which ordinarily offsets only federal income tax liability. Consequently, an early-stage startup or pre-revenue company operating in a net operating loss (NOL) position with no current federal income tax liability cannot derive an immediate cash benefit from the general business credit. That statement is legally incorrect: under IRC §39(a)(1), unused general business credits are carried back one tax year and carried forward 20 tax years (under IRC §39(a)(4), the carryback period is extended to five years specifically for eligible small business credits determined in the first tax year rule where applicable, though the standard general business credit carryforward remains strictly 20 years). The IRS explicitly describes the §41(h) payroll tax credit election as designed to benefit eligible startups that have little or no income tax liability.

Analysis: For a pre-revenue or loss-making technology or life sciences company, a 20-year general business credit carryforward has economic value only if and when the enterprise eventually achieves taxable profitability—and even then, its utilization may be subject to ownership change limitations under IRC §383 following equity financing rounds. By contrast, every startup employing W-2 personnel incurs mandatory employer-side Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) payroll tax liabilities every calendar quarter regardless of profitability. The §41(h) payroll tax offset election converts up to $500,000 per year of otherwise illiquid research credits into an immediate, quarterly reduction of mandatory employer FICA payroll taxes that the company already pays.
Legislative history
PATH Act of 2015

Section 121(c) of the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (enacted as Division Q of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016, P.L. 114-113) permanently extended the IRC §41 research credit and added IRC §41(h) and IRC §3111(f) to the Internal Revenue Code. For tax years beginning after December 31, 2015, and before January 1, 2023, a qualified small business (QSB) could elect to apply up to $250,000 of its annual federal research credit per tax year solely against the employer's 6.2% share of Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI, or Social Security) tax imposed under IRC §3111(a).
Inflation Reduction Act of 2022

Section 13902 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169) expanded the startup payroll tax offset for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022. Specifically, the legislation amended IRC §41(h)(4)(B)(i) and IRC §3111(f) to increase the maximum annual payroll tax credit election by an additional $250,000—raising the total annual cap from $250,000 to $500,000—and permitted the credit to offset the employer's 1.45% share of Hospital Insurance (Medicare) tax imposed under IRC §3111(b) in addition to the 6.2% employer Social Security tax under IRC §3111(a).

cells: Beginning after Dec. 31, 2015 and before Jan. 1, 2023
Employer Social Security tax only (6.2% under IRC §3111(a))
Employer Social Security tax (6.2% under §3111(a), capped at $250,000/quarter), then Employer Medicare tax (1.45% under §3111(b))

body.text: Who qualifies: the qualified small business tests

Under IRC §41(h)(3)(A) and IRS Notice 2017-23 (2017-16 I.R.B. 1100), a corporation (including an S corporation) or a partnership is a qualified small business (QSB) with respect to any tax year if both of the following statutory conditions are satisfied:

items: Current-Year Gross Receipts Threshold: The entity's gross receipts (as determined under the rules of IRC §448(c)(3), without regard to subparagraph (A) thereof) for the election tax year are less than $5,000,000; and

Five-Year Gross Receipts Window (No Prior Gross Receipts Test): The entity did not have gross receipts (as so determined) for any tax year preceding the five-tax-year period ending with the election tax year.

body.text: Under IRC §41(h)(3)(A)(ii) and Notice 2017-23, Section 3.02, any other person (such as an individual operating a sole proprietorship) may also qualify as a QSB if that person satisfies both tests above after taking into account the aggregate gross receipts received by the individual in carrying on all of their trades or businesses.

items: Exclusion of Tax-Exempt Organizations: Under IRC §41(h)(3)(B) and Notice 2017-23, Section 3.03, an organization that is exempt from income taxation under IRC §501 cannot be a qualified small business, even if it otherwise meets the gross receipts tests.

Controlled Group Aggregation: Under IRC §41(h)(5)(A) and Notice 2017-23, Section 3.05, all persons or entities treated as a single taxpayer under the controlled group and common control aggregation rules of IRC §41(f)(1) (incorporating IRC §§52(a), 52(b), 414(m), and 414(o)) are treated as a single taxpayer for purposes of the QSB gross receipts tests and the $500,000 annual election cap. Consequently, gross receipts of all controlled group members must be combined (excluding intercompany transactions) to determine whether the group is under $5 million for the current year and had no gross receipts prior to the five-year window. Furthermore, the $500,000 maximum annual payroll tax credit election is allocated among the members of the controlled group in proportion to each member's share of total qualified research expenses.

body.text: A business incorporated seven years ago that remained completely pre-revenue with zero gross receipts during its first two years can still qualify as a QSB today. Conversely, a company that received any gross receipts six or more tax years earlier fails the test permanently, even if its current-year gross receipts are well below $5 million.

Under Notice 2017-23, Section 3.04, "gross receipts" for purposes of IRC §41(h) are defined by reference to IRC §448(c)(3) and Treas. Reg. §1.448-1T(f)(2)(iv). Under Treas. Reg. §1.448-1T(f)(2)(iv)(A), gross receipts include total sales (net of returns and allowances) and all amounts received for services, as well as any income from investments and from incidental or outside sources—explicitly including interest (including original issue discount and tax-exempt interest), dividends, rents, royalties, and annuities, regardless of whether such amounts are derived in the ordinary course of the taxpayer's trade or business. Note also that under IRC §448(c)(3)(B) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-3(b), if a startup has a short tax year of less than 12 months, gross receipts for that short period must be annualized by multiplying the gross receipts for the short period by 12 and dividing the result by the number of months in the short period.
The Corp A example (Notice 2017-23)

IRS Notice 2017-23, Section 3.06, provides an official administrative example illustrating the operation of the QSB gross receipts rules. In the notice's example, Corp A, a calendar-year C corporation that is neither a §501 tax-exempt organization nor a member of a controlled group, had gross receipts of $1 million in 2012, $7 million in 2013, $4 million in 2014, $3 million in 2015, and $4 million in 2016, and had zero gross receipts for any tax year prior to 2012. Corp A qualifies as a QSB for tax year 2016 because: (1) its gross receipts for 2016 ($4 million) are less than $5 million, and (2) it had no gross receipts before tax year 2012 (which is the start of the five-tax-year period 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016 ending with 2016). Corp A's gross receipts during the intervening years 2012 through 2015—including the $7 million spike in 2013—are legally irrelevant in determining whether Corp A is a QSB for 2016. However, Corp A is disqualified from being a QSB for tax year 2017 (regardless of its 2017 gross receipts), because the five-tax-year period ending with 2017 covers 2013 through 2017, and Corp A had gross receipts in 2012, which falls before that five-year window.
Five-election limit

Under IRC §41(h)(4)(B)(ii), a taxpayer may not make a payroll tax credit election for any tax year if the taxpayer (or any predecessor) has made such an election for five or more preceding tax years. Accordingly, Part 1 of Form 8974 contains exactly five rows to track up to five separate election years. At the current statutory cap of $500,000 per year, making the maximum election across five qualifying tax years can provide up to $2.5 million in total payroll tax offsets—provided all five election tax years begin after December 31, 2022, the company continues to satisfy the QSB tests each year, and the company incurs sufficient QREs each year to generate a $500,000 research credit.
Which expenses generate the credit

Because the payroll tax offset is an election to redirect the IRC §41 research credit, the dollar amount available for the offset depends entirely on the startup's underlying qualified research expenses (QREs).
Categories of qualified research expenses

Under IRC §41(b)(1), total QREs equal the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses" paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the tax year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer.

items: Wages for qualified services (IRC §41(b)(2)(A)(i)): Wages (as defined in IRC §3401(a) for income tax withholding purposes, excluding compensation taken into account in determining the work opportunity credit under §51) paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services." Under IRC §41(b)(2)(B), qualified services consist of: (i) engaging in qualified research, (ii) directly supervising qualified research, or (iii) directly supporting qualified research. Under the "substantially all" rule of IRC §41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80% of an employee's time during the tax year is spent performing qualified services, 100% of that employee's wages qualify as QREs. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" means immediate, first-line supervision (such as a research lab group leader who directly reviews and guides experimental work); higher-level managers and executives to whom first-line supervisors report do not qualify, even if those executives are qualified scientists or engineers.

Supplies used in qualified research (IRC §41(b)(2)(A)(ii)): Any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. Under IRC §41(b)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(b), "supplies" means any tangible property other than: (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Examples include raw materials, electronic components, and laboratory chemicals consumed in fabricating and testing experimental prototypes.

Right to use computers in qualified research (IRC §41(b)(2)(A)(iii)): Under the statutory heading "Right to use computers," in-house research expenses include any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use time-sharing or leased computers in the conduct of qualified research. Because supplies under §41(b)(2)(C) must be tangible property, hosted cloud computing payments (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud compute instances dedicated to staging, simulation, and development environments, as opposed to commercial production web hosting) are properly classified under the separate statutory category of computer rental/lease expenses in IRC §41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(b)(4).

Contract research expenses (IRC §41(b)(3)): Generally, 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research (increased to 75% for payments to qualified research consortia under §41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for certain energy research under §41(b)(3)(D)). Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2), an expense qualifies as contract research only if: (i) the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, (ii) the agreement provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and (iii) the agreement requires the taxpayer to bear the financial expense even if the research is not successful (the economic risk test). Furthermore, under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(a)(3)(i) and §1.41-4A(d), the taxpayer must retain "substantial rights" in the research outcomes. Under IRC §41(d)(4)(F), any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States is strictly excluded from qualified research.

body.text: The four-part test
Under IRC §41(d)(1) as currently in force (following the enactment of P.L. 119-21 on July 4, 2025), "qualified research" is defined by four specific statutory requirements:

items: The Section 174A Expense Test (Elimination of Uncertainty) — IRC §41(d)(1)(A): The research must be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC §174A (Section 70302 of P.L. 119-21 amended §41(d)(1)(A) to refer to §174A rather than former §174 for domestic research in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024). Under Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1), this prong requires that the expenditures be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense—that is, activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process (whether capability, methodology, or appropriate design uncertainty).

Technological in Nature Test — IRC §41(d)(1)(B)(i): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover such information fundamentally relies on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test — IRC §41(d)(1)(B)(ii) & §41(d)(3): The application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (defined in §41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer). Under IRC §41(d)(3)(A), research is conducted for a qualified purpose only if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality. Under IRC §41(d)(3)(B), research is expressly ineligible if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

Process of Experimentation Test — IRC §41(d)(1)(C): Substantially all of the activities (defined in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more of the research activities measured on a cost or another consistently applied reasonable basis) must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under §41(d)(3). Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(5), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities (involving the identification of uncertainty, identification of alternatives, and a systematic process of modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error).

body.text: Internal use software

Under IRC §41(d)(4)(E) and the final Treasury regulations at Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6) (promulgated in T.D. 9786), computer software that is developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for the taxpayer's "internal use" is excluded from qualified research unless it is used in an activity that constitutes qualified research, is used in a production process that meets the requirements of §41(d)(1), or satisfies an additional three-part "high threshold of innovation test."

Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6)(iii), software is presumed to be developed primarily for internal use if it is developed for use in "general and administrative functions" that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business. General and administrative functions are strictly limited to three regulatory categories: (1) financial management functions, (2) human resources management functions, and (3) support services functions (such as data processing, facility services, or marketing/inventory support). Conversely, under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(6)(iv) and (v), software is not internal use software if it is developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or if it is "dual function" or third-party-facing software developed to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system (for example, a customer-facing SaaS platform or e-commerce portal).

cells: The software is innovative in that the software would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement, that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful. This is an objective measurable improvement standard; it does not require the software to be unique or novel to the industry.

The software development involves significant economic risk in that the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period. Technical risk arises from uncertainty in capability, method, or design that cannot be resolved by standard engineering practice.

The software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer in that the software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.

body.text: The shrinking-back rule

Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2), the four-part qualification requirements of IRC §41(d) are applied first at the level of the entire product or overarching business component. If the overall business component as a whole fails to satisfy the four-part test (for example, because less than 80% of the activities on the overall software platform constitute a process of experimentation), the requirements are then applied at the level of the most significant subset of elements of that business component (such as a specific algorithmic subsystem, database engine, or hardware subassembly). This "shrinking back" continues progressively to smaller subsets of elements until either a subset of elements of the business component that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails to satisfy the requirements. Importantly, the shrinking-back rule may be applied only if the overall business component fails the §41(d) requirements.
How the credit is calculated
The Internal Revenue Code provides two distinct methods for computing the research credit.

items: Regular Research Credit (IRC §41(a)(1) & §41(c)): Equals 20% of the excess of the taxpayer's current-year QREs over a statutory "base amount." Under IRC §41(c)(1), the base amount is calculated by multiplying the taxpayer's "fixed-base percentage" by the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer for the four tax years preceding the credit determination year. For "start-up companies" (defined under IRC §41(c)(3)(B)(i) as taxpayers that either had fewer than three tax years between 1984 and 1988 with both gross receipts and QREs, or had their first tax year with both gross receipts and QREs beginning after December 31, 1983), the statutory fixed-base percentage is fixed at 3.0% for each of the taxpayer's first five tax years beginning after 1993 for which it has QREs (§41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(I)), with phased-in historical ratios applying from the sixth through tenth years up to a maximum fixed-base percentage of 16% (§41(c)(3)(C)). Crucially, however, IRC §41(c)(2) imposes a mandatory Minimum Base Amount rule: in no event shall the base amount be less than 50% of the current-year QREs. Because the base amount is floored at 50% of current-year QREs, the maximum excess QREs under the Regular Credit method can never exceed 50% of current-year QREs—meaning the effective Regular Research Credit can never exceed 10% (20% × 50%) of a startup's current-year QREs.

Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) (IRC §41(c)(4)): Under IRC §41(c)(4)(A), a taxpayer may elect to compute its research credit equal to 14% of so much of the current-year QREs as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the three tax years preceding the credit determination year. Under the special startup/no-prior-QRE rule of IRC §41(c)(4)(B), if the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding tax years, the ASC rate is reduced to a flat 6% of current-year QREs (with no base amount subtraction).

Both the 6% rate and the 14% rate are strictly rules of the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC §41(c)(4). Moreover, the 6% ASC rate applies whenever the taxpayer had zero QREs in at least one of the three preceding tax years (which is always true during a startup's first three years of operations, or in any later year following a year with zero QREs), whereas a startup with zero or low gross receipts can simultaneously qualify for the Regular Credit method (yielding up to a 10% effective credit rate on current-year QREs).

In point of law, Congress originally enacted the Alternative Simplified Credit in Section 104(b) of the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 (P.L. 109-432) for tax years ending after December 31, 2006 (initially at a 12% rate), and subsequently increased the ASC rate from 12% to 14% for tax years ending after December 31, 2008, under Section 301(c) of the Tax Extenders and Alternative Minimum Tax Relief Act of 2008 (Division C of P.L. 110-343), while terminating the old Alternative Incremental Research Credit (AIRC) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2008.

body.text: Claiming the offset: the three-step sequence
Step 1: Make the election on Form 6765

The payroll tax credit election is made in Section D of IRS Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities (per the Form 6765 revision released January 2025 and the Instructions for Form 6765 revised December 2025):

items: Line 33a: The taxpayer checks the box on Line 33a to affirmatively elect to claim a portion of its research credit as a qualified small business payroll tax credit. (Line 33b is checked if the payroll tax is reported under a different Employer Identification Number (EIN), such as through a third-party payer).
Line 34: The taxpayer enters the portion of the research credit it elects to claim as a payroll tax credit, subject to the statutory maximum of $500,000.
Line 35: Taxpayers other than partnerships and S corporations enter their general business credit carryforward from the current year (determined via the worksheet in the Form 6765 instructions).

Line 36: The taxpayer determines the final allowable payroll tax credit—which for C corporations and individuals is the smallest of Line 28 (total current-year research credit after §280C election), Line 34 (elected amount up to $500,000), or Line 35 (general business credit carryforward from the current year), and for partnerships and S corporations is the smaller of Line 28 or Line 34—and carries this Line 36 amount to Form 8974, Part 1, column (e).

body.text: Under IRC §41(h)(4)(A)(i) and Notice 2017-23, Section 4.02, Form 6765 containing the completed Section D election must be attached to the taxpayer's timely filed original federal income tax return (such as Form 1120, Form 1120-S, Form 1065, or Form 1040) for the tax year to which the election applies, including extensions (specifically, on or before the due date, including extensions, of that return). Under IRC §41(h)(4)(A)(ii), once made, the payroll tax credit election may be revoked only with the consent of the Secretary of the Treasury (the IRS). Under IRC §41(h)(4)(C), in the case of a partnership or an S corporation, the election to take the payroll tax credit is made strictly at the entity level.

While IRS Notice 2017-23, Section 4.02, provided a one-time administrative transition rule allowing QSBs that had already filed their 2016 returns on or before April 10, 2017, to make the payroll tax election on an amended return filed on or before December 31, 2017, that transitional window expired on December 31, 2017. Today, if a startup files its original income tax return without making the Section D payroll election on Form 6765 (and does not file a superseding return prior to the extended due date), the ability to monetize that year's research credit against payroll taxes is permanently forfeited; even if the startup later amends its return to claim the §41 research credit, that credit can only be used as a standard income tax credit subject to the IRC §39 one-year carryback and 20-year carryforward rules.
The section 280C(c) election: update
That 2017 guidance predated both the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) §174 capitalization regime (2022–2024) and the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025).

Under IRC §280C(c) as amended by Section 70302 of P.L. 119-21 (effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, with an optional retroactive transition election available for eligible small businesses meeting the §448(c) gross receipts test back to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021):

items: Without the §280C(c)(2) Reduced Credit Election (Full Credit Claimed): Under IRC §280C(c)(1), the taxpayer claims 100% of its computed §41 research credit (maximizing the dollar amount transferred to Form 6765 Section D for the payroll tax offset), but the taxpayer must reduce the amount of its domestic research or experimental expenditure deduction allowable under IRC §174A(a) (or the amount chargeable to capital account under §174A(c) if amortized) by 100% of the research credit claimed. Note that per the Form 6765 instructions, any portion of the research credit elected as a payroll tax credit under §41(h) is treated as a research credit for purposes of §280C(c).

With the §280C(c)(2) Reduced Credit Election: The taxpayer elects on its timely filed original return (on Line 17 for Section A Regular Credit or Line 30 for Section B ASC on Form 6765) to reduce its current-year §41 research credit by the product of the credit and the maximum corporate tax rate under IRC §11(b) (currently 21%). Consequently, the taxpayer receives 79% of the unreduced research credit, and its domestic research deduction under IRC §174A is not reduced. Under IRC §280C(c)(2)(C), this election must be made on a timely filed original return (including extensions) and is irrevocable.

body.text: Analysis: For a cash-constrained startup in a tax loss position, declining the §280C(c)(2) election still produces a 26.58% larger research credit (100% vs. 79% of the gross credit), and therefore yields a substantially larger immediate payroll tax cash offset (unless the startup's reduced credit already exceeds the $500,000 annual payroll offset cap, in which case electing §280C(c)(2) preserves the full $500,000 payroll offset and avoids reducing the §174A deduction). When the gross credit is below $500,000, the trade-off of claiming the unreduced credit is a dollar-for-dollar reduction in the startup's current-year §174A deduction, which reduces the startup's net operating loss (NOL) carryforward for future profitable years (where that NOL would otherwise shield income at the 21% corporate tax rate). Because an immediate dollar of payroll tax savings today is worth 100 cents on the dollar, whereas a dollar of reduced §174A deduction reduces a future NOL tax shield by only 21 cents on the dollar (discounted for time and probability of profitability), startups generating less than $500,000 in gross research credits generally still maximize economic value by claiming the full credit and reducing their §174A deduction.
Step 2: Wait for the first quarter that begins after filing

Under IRC §3111(f)(1), IRC §3111(f)(2), and Notice 2017-23, Section 4.04, the payroll tax credit election applies to wages paid in the first calendar quarter that begins after the date on which the taxpayer files its federal income tax return making the Form 6765 election. A taxpayer cannot apply the payroll tax credit to the calendar quarter in which the income tax return is filed, nor retroactively to prior quarters.

headers: First quarter for the payroll credit

cells: Second Quarter of 2025 (Form 941 filed by July 31, 2025)

body.text: Step 3: Claim the credit on Form 8974 and the payroll return

To apply the credit against payroll taxes, the startup completes IRS Form 8974, Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities (Instructions revised December 2024), and attaches it to its employment tax return—typically Form 941, Employer's QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return (or Form 943, Employer's Annual Federal Tax Return for Agricultural Employees, or Form 944, Employer's ANNUAL Federal Tax Return).
In Part 2 of Form 8974, the credit is applied in a strict statutory two-tier ordering sequence under IRC §3111(f)(1) and (2):

items: First Tier — Employer Social Security Tax (Lines 8–11 of Form 8974): The available credit is applied first against the employer's 6.2% share of Social Security tax for the quarter. Crucially, under IRC §3111(f)(1) and Line 11 of Form 8974, the credit applied against the employer's share of Social Security tax cannot exceed $250,000 in any single calendar quarter on Form 941 (or $1,000,000 per year for annual filers on Form 943 or Form 944).

Second Tier — Employer Medicare Tax (Lines 12–16 of Form 8974): Any remaining elected credit that was not used against employer Social Security tax in step 1 (either because the startup's quarterly employer Social Security tax liability was less than its available credit, or because the startup hit the $250,000 quarterly Social Security cap on Line 11) is then applied on Lines 12 through 16 against the employer's 1.45% share of Medicare tax for that same quarter.

Total Payroll Tax Credit (Line 17 of Form 8974): The sum of the Social Security offset (Line 12) and the Medicare offset (Line 16) is entered on Line 17 of Form 8974 and carried to Form 941, Part 1, Line 11a.

body.text: That phrasing is inaccurate under post-2022 law. While the annual election limit per tax year is $500,000, the $250,000 figure on Form 8974 (Line 11) is strictly the per-quarter ceiling on the employer Social Security tax portion of the offset. If a high-payroll startup has elected the full $500,000 credit (or has accumulated carryovers from multiple election years on Part 1 of Form 8974) and has more than $250,000 in quarterly employer Social Security tax alongside substantial employer Medicare tax, the startup can offset $250,000 of employer Social Security tax plus its full employer Medicare tax liability in the very same quarter—exceeding $250,000 in total quarterly benefit.
Limits and carryovers

Under IRC §3111(f)(3), the payroll tax credit is non-refundable. The credit claimed for any calendar quarter cannot exceed the sum of the employer's share of Social Security tax (under §3111(a)) and the employer's share of Medicare tax (under §3111(b)) imposed on wages paid during that quarter. It cannot be used to offset employee-withheld FICA taxes, federal income tax withholding, Additional Medicare Tax withholding, or Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) taxes.

Under IRC §3111(f)(3)(B), if the amount of the elected payroll tax credit exceeds the employer's Social Security and Medicare tax liability for a calendar quarter, the unused excess is carried over to the succeeding calendar quarter (and subsequent quarters indefinitely until fully exhausted, or to the succeeding calendar year for annual Form 943/944 filers) and allowed as a payroll tax credit in those succeeding periods subject to the same statutory limitations. As confirmed by IRS guidance and the Form 8974 instructions, any unused credit elected for tax years beginning before January 1, 2023, that is carried forward into calendar quarters beginning after December 31, 2022, may now be applied first against employer Social Security tax (up to $250,000 per quarter) and then against employer Medicare tax.

Additionally, under IRC §3111(f)(4), the credit allowed under §3111(f) is not taken into account for purposes of determining the amount of any deduction allowed under Chapter 1 of the Internal Revenue Code for taxes paid under §3111. This means the startup retains its full ordinary business income tax deduction under IRC §162 for the employer FICA payroll taxes, unreduced by the Form 8974 credit.
Professional employer organizations and other aggregate filers

Many startups outsource human resources and payroll administration to a Professional Employer Organization (PEO), a Certified Professional Employer Organization (CPEO), or an IRC §3504 reporting agent that files an aggregate Form 941 under the third-party payer's own EIN.
Under Notice 2017-23, Section 4.06, and the Instructions for Form 8974 and Schedule R (Form 941), the procedural mechanics for startups using third-party payers are as follows:

items: The startup client must first make the payroll tax credit election on Form 6765 (checking both Line 33a and Line 33b to indicate payroll taxes are reported under a different EIN) attached to the startup's own timely filed federal income tax return.

Beginning in the first calendar quarter after the startup files its income tax return, the CPEO, §3504 agent, or non-certified PEO attaches a separate Form 8974 completed specifically for that startup client, along with Schedule R (Form 941), Allocation Schedule for Aggregate Form 941 Filers, to the third-party payer's aggregate Form 941, allocating the credit to the startup client's wages and reducing the startup's required payroll funding remittance accordingly.

body.text: Interaction with the alternative minimum tax
In addition to enacting the payroll tax offset, Section 121(b) of the PATH Act of 2015 enacted permanent Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) relief for "eligible small businesses."

Under IRC §38(c)(4)(B)(ii), for tax years beginning after December 31, 2015, the IRC §41 research credit determined with respect to an eligible small business is classified as a "specified credit." Under IRC §38(c)(4)(A), in computing the general business credit limitation against income tax, the tentative minimum tax is treated as being zero for specified credits—allowing an eligible small business (and its pass-through partners or S corporation shareholders) to apply the research credit against both regular income tax and Alternative Minimum Tax. Under IRC §38(c)(5)(A) (redesignated from former §38(c)(5)(C) by P.L. 115-141 in 2018), an "eligible small business" is defined as a corporation whose stock is not publicly traded, a partnership, or a sole proprietorship, provided that the average annual gross receipts of such corporation, partnership, or sole proprietorship for the three-tax-year period preceding the tax year of the credit do not exceed $50,000,000 (applying the controlled group aggregation and §448(c)(3) rules). (Note also that the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 repealed the corporate AMT for C corporations beginning in 2018, while the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 enacted a separate 15% Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax on corporations with average annual adjusted financial statement income exceeding $1 billion—making §38(c)(4)(B)(ii) primarily relevant today to individual founders, partners, and S corporation shareholders subject to the individual AMT).

That is a reversal of the statutory formula in IRC §38(c)(1). Under IRC §38(c)(1), the general business credit allowed for any tax year cannot exceed the excess of the taxpayer's "net income tax" over the greater of:

items: (A) the tentative minimum tax for the tax year (which is treated as $0 for an eligible small business's research credit under §38(c)(4)(A)), or
(B) 25 percent of so much of the taxpayer's net regular tax liability as exceeds $25,000.

body.text: Thus, 25% of net regular tax liability above $25,000 is the statutory floor below which the credit cannot reduce income tax—meaning an eligible small business can use its research credit to offset 100% of the first $25,000 of net regular tax liability plus 75% of all net regular tax liability exceeding $25,000 (leaving 25% of the tax above $25,000 payable). Furthermore, this §38(c) AMT rule governs income tax credit utilization and is wholly distinct from the §41(h) payroll tax offset, which is not subject to the §38(c)(1) 25% net regular tax floor.
Compliance and audit risk
Correction on "Tier 1" compliance issue status

That statement is outdated by more than a decade. While the IRS Large and Mid-Size Business (LMSB, now Large Business and International, or LB&I) division placed the Research Credit Claims issue into "Tier I" of its Issue Tiering management system in 2007, LB&I formally abolished the entire Tiered Issue Management process on August 17, 2012, via LB&I Directive LB&I-04-0812-010 (Discontinuation of Tiered Issue Management), replacing it with Knowledge Management networks (Issue Practice Groups). Subsequently, on February 27, 2020, the IRS LB&I division launched a dedicated "Research Issues" Compliance Campaign specifically targeting IRC §41 and §174 research claims through issue-based examinations, centralized risk assessment directives (such as LB&I-04-0920-0016), soft letters, and enhanced promoter scrutiny.
Per-project / Business component substantiation (Form 6765 Section G)

On the administrative filing side, the IRS revamped Form 6765 (released January 2025, with revised Instructions issued December 2025) by adding Section G (Business Component Information). Under the December 2025 Form 6765 instructions, completing Section G—which requires granular quantitative and qualitative reporting by individual business component covering at least 80% of total QREs across up to the top 50 business components—is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (including 2025 tax returns). Furthermore, for tax years beginning after 2025, the IRS Form 6765 instructions explicitly exempt two categories of taxpayers from mandatory Section G reporting on the return itself:

items: Qualified Small Businesses (QSBs) electing the payroll tax credit under Section D of Form 6765; and
Taxpayers with total QREs of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less (determined at the controlled group level).

body.text: Even where a startup is exempt from completing Section G on the face of Form 6765 when filing its original return, Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) and IRC §6001 strictly require the startup to maintain contemporaneous books and records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that each business component meets the four-part test and to tie employee wages, supplies, computer rental, and contract research costs to those qualifying components upon IRS examination.
Correction on UK HMRC audit statistics

An audit of HMRC's official published reports shows that those figures do not match HMRC's actual published statistics. In HMRC's official publication, HMRC's approach to Research and Development tax reliefs 2023 to 2024, HMRC reported that under its second Mandatory Random Enquiry Programme (MREP) covering 2021 to 2022 claims, approximately half of SME scheme claims were non-compliant in part or in full, with 30% found to be fully non-compliant (no qualifying R&D present) and a further 21% found to be partially non-compliant (combined 51% non-compliance rate among randomly sampled SME claims). Additionally, HMRC's published overall error and fraud rate estimates by value for the UK SME R&D scheme were 24.4% for 2020–21, 25.8% for 2021–22, 19.5% for 2022–23 (projected), and 14.6% for 2023–24 (illustrative). Importantly, these UK HMRC statistics measure compliance under the United Kingdom's Corporation Tax Act 2009 R&D relief schemes and do not measure U.S. IRS audit disallowance rates under IRC §41.
Worked example (hypothetical): Startup XYZ, recomputed

While Startup XYZ's qualification as a QSB is legally valid (assuming its first year of any gross receipts was 2023, placing it within its five-year gross receipts window and below the $5,000,000 current-year ceiling), a $100,000 credit on $500,000 of QREs is mathematically impossible under the Internal Revenue Code. As established in the calculation section above, under the minimum base amount rule of IRC §41(c)(2), a taxpayer's base amount under the Regular Credit method can never be less than 50% of current-year QREs ($250,000), which caps the maximum Regular Credit at 10% of current-year QREs ($50,000).

The statutory recomputation below applies the exact formulas of IRC §41(a), §41(c)(2), §41(c)(4), and §280C(c) to Startup XYZ's $500,000 of 2025 QREs (assuming Startup XYZ had zero QREs in at least one of the three preceding years 2022–2024, or that its start-up 3% fixed-base percentage times average prior gross receipts is below the 50% minimum base, and that Startup XYZ timely files its 2025 calendar-year Form 1120 on April 15, 2026):

cells: 20% × $250,000 excess QREs (10% effective rate on total QREs)
6% × $500,000 current-year QREs (assuming no QREs in at least one of prior 3 years)

body.text: Suppose Startup XYZ selects the Regular Credit method without making the §280C(c)(2) reduced credit election, yielding a $50,000 research credit on Form 6765, and elects in Section D (Lines 33a–36) to apply the entire $50,000 as a payroll tax credit. Under IRC §280C(c)(1), because Startup XYZ did not make the reduced credit election, it must reduce its 2025 domestic research expenditure deduction under IRC §174A by $50,000 (from $500,000 to $450,000).

Because Startup XYZ files its 2025 income tax return on April 15, 2026 (which falls during the second calendar quarter of 2026), the first calendar quarter in which Startup XYZ may apply the payroll tax credit on Form 8974 and Form 941 is the Third Quarter of 2026 (July 1, 2026 to September 30, 2026, with Form 941 due by November 2, 2026). Assume Startup XYZ pays $400,000 in covered W-2 wages during Q3 2026, with no individual employee exceeding the annual Social Security wage base:

cells: 6.2% × $400,000 Q3 wages (well under the $250,000 quarterly OASDI cap on Form 8974 Line 11)
Remaining Credit Available for Tier 2 in Q3 2026
$50,000 elected credit − $24,800 Social Security tax offset
1.45% × $400,000 Q3 wages (applied against remaining $25,200 credit on Form 8974 Line 16)
Total Payroll Tax Credit Utilized in Q3 2026 (Form 8974 Line 17)
$24,800 Social Security offset + $5,800 Medicare offset (7.65% of $400,000 wages)
Unused Excess Credit Carried Forward to Q4 2026 (§3111(f)(3)(B))
$50,000 total elected credit − $30,600 used in Q3 2026

body.text: State research credits

In addition to the federal IRC §41 research credit and §41(h) payroll tax offset, more than 35 U.S. states offer state-level research and development tax incentives (though state-level mechanisms vary between non-refundable income tax credits, refundable credits, and state payroll withholding offsets such as in Georgia). State research credits are governed by state revenue statutes and operate independently of the federal Form 6765 / Form 8974 payroll tax election.
